papers.abstract: Model-guided directed evolution seeks to identify high-fitness protein variants under limited oracle budgets. Protein language models (PLMs) provide rich representations for this task, but task-agnostic zero-shot scores can be misaligned with a target assay, while supervised search in high-dimensional embedding spaces can make surrogate modeling and uncertainty estimation sample-inefficient. We propose the Linear Fitness Subspace (LFS) hypothesis: within mutation-induced residue-level representation changes, a compact, assay-specific set of directions makes fitness variation linearly accessible from few labeled variants. This is a local, supervision-recoverable statement rather than a claim that protein fitness landscapes or global PLM geometry are universally linear. Building on this observation, we introduce Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES), which estimates an LFS from a small initial sample and performs surrogate modeling, uncertainty estimation, and acquisition in the learned subspace. Across 10 core ProteinGym assays, 87 extended static-validation assays, and an 18-assay budgeted-search evaluation, SGES improves fitness prediction and search efficiency over zero-shot PLMs and recent ML-guided protein optimization baselines. Controlled comparisons with PCA, random projections, label-shuffled PLS, classical mutation features, and acquisition ablations further isolate the benefit of a fitness-aligned site-delta coordinate.

papers.title: AcrSeek: metric learning with hybrid negative mining for anti-CRISPR protein detection under extreme class imbalance.
papers.abstract: Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins inhibit CRISPR-Cas immunity and are key targets for precise control of CRISPR-based genome editing and phage-host coevolution research. Their experimental identification is costly and low-throughput, so computational predictors are used to prioritise candidates for testing. In this setting validated positives number in the hundreds while phage-derived putative negatives reach tens of thousands, producing extreme class imbalance. Yet existing classification-based predictors train and evaluate on 1:1 balanced datasets and allow high-similarity sequences between training and test, overestimating real-world performance. We present AcrSeek, a metric-learning framework that trains a projection head over a frozen protein language model (PLM) encoder with hybrid negative mining (offline global plus online semi-hard) under a joint triplet-focal objective. Under nested 5-fold cross-validation with leakage controlled by 40% identity clustering, AcrSeek improved AUPRC on the imbalanced (1:383) test set from 0.017 to 0.355 over AcrNET (matched PLM backbone), reaching 0.508 with ESM-2 3B. AcrSeek therefore remains structurally robust under extreme class imbalance and may also serve other protein-function detection problems with scarce positives. Source code at https://github.com/jeongchans/acrseek, archived at Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21946803); data and model checkpoints at Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20115442).

papers.title: Language models annotate mass cytometry clusters within the range where human experts disagree
papers.abstract: Cell-type identification of clusters from unsupervised cytometry pipelines (e.g. FlowSOM, GigaSOM) is a time-consuming, expert-dependent bottleneck, typically requiring an expert to read a heatmap of median marker intensities and assign a label to each cluster. Large language models (LLMs) can annotate single-cell RNA-seq clusters from marker-gene lists, but cytometry cluster data differ in both dimensionality and data type. We present a direct procedure in which cluster medians are scaled per marker and grouped by similarity into a few dozen metaclusters. The continuous marker profiles are then passed to the LLM, which returns a cell-type label and confidence level for each metacluster in a single call, without a gating hierarchy, manually defined marker-specific thresholds, or task-specific training data. Across four human and mouse datasets spanning blood, bone marrow and gut, a single well-chosen model reproduces the reference annotation at the major-lineage level with 85-98% metacluster-level concordance (cloud Claude Sonnet 4.6 85-98%, best local model 83-96%), substantially exceeding majority-class baselines; chance-corrected agreement is Cohen's k = 0.67-0.83. Local open-weight models perform competitively with the cloud model on the independent benchmarks, enabling application to clinical or patient-derived data subject to data-protection restrictions. Reliability is model-dependent: no local model is best everywhere, and the frontier model Claude Opus 5 was no more reliable than Claude Sonnet 4.6, the most consistent in concordance across datasets. Because no annotation is absolute ground truth, we obtained two additional expert annotations of the same continuous heatmaps, blinded to the reference and to all model output, to establish a method-matched agreement ceiling. The experts agreed on ~99% of major-lineage assignments but only ~73% of T-cell maturation states; on that axis the best models fall within the expert disagreement range. LLM-based annotation is therefore a practical, training-free alternative to rule-based annotation, provided its output is checked against the intended panel and species.

papers.title: THItoGene: a deep learning method for predicting spatial transcriptomics from histological images
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics unveils the complex dynamics of cell regulation and transcriptomes, but it is typically cost-prohibitive. Predicting spatial gene expression from histological images via artificial intelligence offers a more affordable option, yet existing methods fall short in extracting deep-level information from pathological images. In this paper, we present THItoGene, a hybrid neural network that utilizes dynamic convolutional and capsule networks to adaptively sense potential molecular signals in histological images for exploring the relationship between high-resolution pathology image phenotypes and regulation of gene expression. A comprehensive benchmark evaluation using datasets from human breast cancer and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma has demonstrated the superior performance of THItoGene in spatial gene expression prediction. Moreover, THItoGene has demonstrated its capacity to decipher both the spatial context and enrichment signals within specific tissue regions. THItoGene can be freely accessed at https://github.com/yrjia1015/THItoGene.

papers.title: GenSLMs: Genome-scale language models reveal SARS-CoV-2 evolutionary dynamics
papers.abstract: We seek to transform how new and emergent variants of pandemic-causing viruses, specifically SARS-CoV-2, are identified and classified. By adapting large language models (LLMs) for genomic data, we build genome-scale language models (GenSLMs) which can learn the evolutionary landscape of SARS-CoV-2 genomes. By pre-training on over 110 million prokaryotic gene sequences and fine-tuning a SARS-CoV-2-specific model on 1.5 million genomes, we show that GenSLMs can accurately and rapidly identify variants of concern. Thus, to our knowledge, GenSLMs represents one of the first whole genome scale foundation models which can generalize to other prediction tasks. We demonstrate scaling of GenSLMs on GPU-based supercomputers and AI-hardware accelerators utilizing 1.63 Zettaflops in training runs with a sustained performance of 121 PFLOPS in mixed precision and peak of 850 PFLOPS. We present initial scientific insights from examining GenSLMs in tracking evolutionary dynamics of SARS-CoV-2, paving the path to realizing this on large biological data.
papers.venue: The International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications

papers.title: Integrated analysis of multimodal single-cell data with structural similarity
papers.abstract: Multimodal single-cell sequencing technologies provide unprecedented information on cellular heterogeneity from multiple layers of genomic readouts. However, joint analysis of two modalities without properly handling the noise often leads to overfitting of one modality by the other and worse clustering results than vanilla single-modality analysis. How to efficiently utilize the extra information from single cell multi-omics to delineate cell states and identify meaningful signal remains as a significant computational challenge. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework, named SAILERX, for efficient, robust, and flexible analysis of multi-modal single-cell data. SAILERX consists of a variational autoencoder with invariant representation learning to correct technical noises from sequencing process, and a multimodal data alignment mechanism to integrate information from different modalities. Instead of performing hard alignment by projecting both modalities to a shared latent space, SAILERX encourages the local structures of two modalities measured by pairwise similarities to be similar. This strategy is more robust against overfitting of noises, which facilitates various downstream analysis such as clustering, imputation, and marker gene detection. Furthermore, the invariant representation learning part enables SAILERX to perform integrative analysis on both multi- and single-modal datasets, making it an applicable and scalable tool for more general scenarios.

papers.title: Generative modeling of single-cell time series with PRESCIENT enables prediction of cell trajectories with interventions
papers.abstract: Existing computational methods that use single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) for cell fate prediction do not model how cells evolve stochastically and in physical time, nor can they predict how differentiation trajectories are altered by proposed interventions. We introduce PRESCIENT (Potential eneRgy undErlying Single Cell gradIENTs), a generative modeling framework that learns an underlying differentiation landscape from time-series scRNA-seq data. We validate PRESCIENT on an experimental lineage tracing dataset, where we show that PRESCIENT is able to predict the fate biases of progenitor cells in hematopoiesis when accounting for cell proliferation, improving upon the best-performing existing method. We demonstrate how PRESCIENT can simulate trajectories for perturbed cells, recovering the expected effects of known modulators of cell fate in hematopoiesis and pancreatic β cell differentiation. PRESCIENT is able to accommodate complex perturbations of multiple genes, at different time points and from different starting cell populations, and is available at https://github.com/gifford-lab/prescient .

papers.title: Biobank-scale self-supervised genotype pretraining yields transferable representations for human genetics.
papers.abstract: Biobank-scale genotyping has created unprecedented cohorts for human genetics, yet the field still lacks scalable methods for learning transferable representations from largely unlabeled individual-level genotype data. Here, we introduce SNPBERT, a self-supervised transformer pretrained on genotypes from 485 923 UK Biobank participants using masked rsID prediction. SNPBERT embeddings recovered known population structure across UK Biobank and three external datasets, performed comparably to principal component analysis, and supported the identification of ancestry-informative marker SNPs. Fine-tuning with an attention-based multiple-instance head generated disease-specific risk scores that provided complementary information beyond conventional polygenic risk scores. The relative increase in Nagelkerke's R2 ranged from 0.7% to 3.3%, and independent associations were observed for seven of the eight chronic diseases examined. In celiac disease, attention prioritization recapitulated major histocompatibility complex signals while elevating variants in CCHCR1 and NOTCH4 relative to genome-wide association study (GWAS) ranking. These results support biobank-scale genotype pretraining as an early step toward foundation modeling for individual-level genotype data.

papers.title: Protein resource allocation across subcellular compartments revealed by large-scale absolute quantitative proteomics in yeast.
papers.abstract: Subcellular compartmentalization within complex membrane-bound organelles is a hallmark of eukaryal life, enabling metabolic specialization through spatial segregation. Here, we compiled a dataset encompassing 300 absolute quantitative proteomes, the largest to date, across two yeast species under diverse experimental conditions. Leveraging big data analysis, formula fitting, and machine learning, quantitative correlations among protein abundance, resource allocation, and cellular phenotypes were elucidated at a system level. We found that subcellular resource distribution is highly uneven and covaries with specific growth rate. Specifically, at high specific growth rates, the protein mass fraction (PMF) from certain compartments, (e.g., nucleus) is consistently reduced, coinciding with the increasing protein resource demand from ribosomes. Meanwhile, nutrient limitation may induce resource recycling by upregulating protein resources within specific compartments (e.g., vacuole) to sustain stress adaptation. Importantly, our integrative analysis indicates that PMF from a few subcellular compartments (e.g., nucleus and ribosomes) can accurately predict yeast physiological parameters (e.g., specific growth rate, oxygen uptake rate), and a limited protein set (≥ 23) could be used to capture the variation in resource allocation across seven major subcellular compartments. Furthermore, our comparative analysis between Crabtree-positive and Crabtree-negative species across conditions illustrates that subcellular resource allocation could be shaped by multiple factors and the two species differ markedly in their robustness to environmental perturbations. In summary, the high-quality quantitative proteomic dataset for yeast species offers an unprecedented opportunity for understanding the general principles underlying subcellular resource allocation, laying foundations for precision engineering of cell factories in synthetic biology.
papers.venue: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

papers.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts.
papers.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

papers.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
papers.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

papers.title: Deep learning uncovers hidden power of low-affinity motifs.
papers.abstract: Low-affinity transcription factor binding sites are functionally important but difficult to map and mechanistically poorly understood. In this issue of Cell Genomics, Weilert et al. leverage sequence-to-function deep learning models to systematically map low-affinity pioneer factor binding sites in mouse embryonic stem cells and reveal how these sites contribute to chromatin opening through soft-syntax nucleosomal cooperativity.

papers.title: CMGL: confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning for cancer subtype classification.
papers.abstract: Multi-omics integration can improve cancer subtyping, but modality informativeness and noise vary across cancer types and patients. Most graph methods for multi-omics data learn modality contributions within the downstream classification objective, leaving predictive reliability for each patient implicit. As a result, uninformative modalities can weaken the fused representation, while unreliable omics can introduce noisy patient relationships into graph propagation. To address these two problems, we propose confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning (CMGL), which produces a separate reliability estimate before fusion and uses consensus patient neighborhoods for graph classification. CMGL estimates modality confidence for each patient through evidential deep learning, fixes these values during fusion across omics, and performs classification on an independently specified consistency graph. On four MLOmics cancer-subtype tasks and the 32-class pan-cancer task, CMGL consistently improves over the strongest baseline, surpassing it by 4.03% in average accuracy on the four single-cancer tasks. Its representations recover the PAM50 intrinsic subtypes of breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA), and the model trained on BRCA transfers without fine tuning to kidney renal clear cell carcinoma, stratifying patients into prognostically distinct groups. The code is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21921069.

papers.title: FunFOLD5: combining localised templates and structural homology for accurate predictions of biologically relevant protein-ligand interactions.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in protein-ligand modelling is to predict not only the presence of an interaction but also the correct ligand identity, binding-site location, and biologically relevant bound conformation. While recent deep learning approaches such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 have demonstrated impressive accuracy in modelling protein-ligand complexes, these methods typically require prior knowledge of the ligand, focus on a single dominant binding pose, and rely heavily on large training datasets. Template-based methods offer a complementary solution by leveraging experimentally resolved protein-ligand complexes to transfer both binding-site architecture and ligand chemical identity, enabling function inference even for uncharacterised or engineered proteins. However, conventional template-based methods are limited by their dependence on global fold similarity, which can miss local binding features critical for ligand specificity. Localised template search strategies may overcome this limitation by capturing conserved pocket-level interactions, enabling more accurate and functionally relevant ligand-binding predictions across diverse protein families. We present FunFOLD5, a template-based method for predicting protein-ligand binding sites. Whereas its predecessor FunFOLD4 relied on global fold similarity to identify templates, FunFOLD5 combines local and global searches, integrating rapid structural template retrieval with a local targeted protocol to improve interaction accuracy. The pipeline combines Foldseek-based template searching, curated ligand annotations from BioLiP2, and ligand superposition followed by spatial clustering to identify associated ligands and consensus binding sites. Benchmarking on blind targets from CASP15 and CASP16 demonstrates robust performance across a wide range of biologically relevant ligands, including nucleotides, metal ions, cofactors, and small metabolites. FunFOLD5 achieved high-accuracy predictions for 81.2% of ligand instances (56 of 69). Importantly, the local targeted protocol consistently improved ligand identification, residue-level recall, and binding-pose accuracy. FunFOLD5 is freely available as a Dockerised pipeline at https://hub.docker.com/r/radiyaman/funfold5_template, providing a scalable and reproducible framework for large-scale protein-ligand interaction analysis and functional annotation.

papers.title: Natural variation in GmRVE4d facilitates soybean latitudinal adaptation by regulating GmPRR5a-dependent flowering and maturity.
papers.abstract: Timely flowering and maturity are crucial for plant reproduction and environmental adaptation. Light-dark cycle-associated regulatory networks integrate photoperiodic cues with intrinsic developmental programs and play pivotal roles in flowering, maturity and environmental adaptation. Soybean is a short-day crop with strong photoperiod responsiveness; however, the molecular mechanisms by which these networks mediate soybean adaptation to diverse environments remain largely elusive. Here, we combine genome-wide association analysis with deep learning-based assessment of soybean maturity variation and identify GmRVE4d, a homolog of the Arabidopsis clock-associated REVEILLE, as a maturity-associated locus across both field environments. Genetic analysis reveals evidence of domestication-related artificial selection at GmRVE4d and identifies the late-maturing haplotype GmRVE4dH3. Functional analyses further demonstrate that the GmRVE4d protein directly binds to the promoter of GmPRR5a, a soybean homolog of the Arabidopsis clock-associated component PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR 5, and represses its transcription, thereby delaying soybean flowering and maturity. Taken together, our findings suggest that GmRVE4d is a negative regulator of soybean flowering and maturity that functions by directly repressing GmPRR5a expression and represents a promising molecular target for expanding cultivation latitudes through molecular breeding.

papers.title: Shared patterns of human milk composition link mammary gland function to infant growth.
papers.abstract: The mammary gland produces nutrient-rich human milk (HM), yet how mammary functional state shapes HM composition and infant outcomes remains poorly understood. We used HM multi-omics - metabolomics, proteomics, micronutrients, macronutrients, and HM oligosaccharides - across 1,543 samples from three cohorts, including two randomized trials, as a noninvasive readout of mammary functional state. Trajectory modeling and multi-omic integration showed that maternal supplementation improved recovery from early growth faltering and revealed a shared HM compositional axis linking maternal nutrition to infant growth. Machine learning, with Human Protein Atlas-informed proteomics, identified seven HM biomarkers reflecting variation across key mammary domains, indexing milk synthesis, barrier integrity, and immune/repair activity. Elevated valerylcarnitine and low pantothenic acid emerged as metabolic signals linking mammary functional state to infant growth.

papers.title: RandomReadsMG: Rapid, realistic metagenome simulation at terabase scale for benchmarking and experimental design.
papers.abstract: Realistic synthetic metagenomes are essential for benchmarking bioinformatics tools, guiding experimental design, and generating labeled data for artificial intelligence and machine learning. We present RandomReadsMG, an open-source metagenomic read simulator distributed with BBTools. It generates communities containing hundreds to 50,000 genomes in a single command and supports user-defined abundance profiles, configurable within-genome coverage variation, retained read provenance, sequencing errors, and library artifacts. Presets are provided for Illumina, Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), and PacBio sequencing. In benchmarks, RandomReadsMG produced terabase-scale datasets in under 6 h while maintaining bounded memory use. Simulations based on empirical drinking water profiles preserved genome-level depth after remapping. Controlled pathogen spike-ins further showed how simulation can estimate thresholds for read detection and metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) recovery. RandomReadsMG provides a fast, reproducible framework for metagenomics benchmarking, biosurveillance study design, and large-scale synthetic data generation.

papers.title: Keep AI-augmented science contestable.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving upstream in science. Systems such as AlphaFold have already transformed protein-structure prediction, while newer agentic systems can search literatures, generate hypotheses, write and execute code, interpret results, and automate much of the path from idea to paper. Recent debates have asked how such systems may change scientific progress, surprise, and human understanding. Yet they also change something more fundamental: who-or what-participates in deciding which questions are asked, which evidence is surfaced, and which alternatives survive. As machine intelligence becomes part of science's epistemic infrastructure, steps must be taken to ensure that researchers who did not build, own, or operate the system can still contest how ideas and evidence became a claim.

papers.title: Scarless regeneration requires post-translational proteolytic regulation via macrophage-derived Legumain
papers.abstract: Macrophages express proteolytic factors in response to injury but how proteases are deployed and regulated during regeneration are incompletely defined. Beyond their transcriptomic expression, activity of individual proteases is defined both by their unique substrate specificity and post-translational modifications of their active forms. Here we show a key role for the lysosomal protease Legumain in controlling ECM dynamics and post-translational processing of the regenerative proteome. Injury interface-targeted Ctsla localization and post-translational processing requires Lgmn in macrophages. Extracellular cues from physical remodeling control differentiation state and injury response of ligament resident fibroblasts. Loss of ECM turnover, including localized Fibronectin 1a/b remodeling, impairs dedifferentiation in legumain mutants and leads to fibrotic scarring. Taken together, we demonstrate a role for macrophage-derived lysosomal proteases as specialized tools required to fine-tune proteome composition and function in regeneration.

papers.title: Data mining of global sequence datasets markedly expands known diversity within the Tobamovirus genus
papers.abstract: High-throughput sequencing has transformed RNA virus discovery, producing vast datasets that often contain unexplored sequences of known and novel viruses across diverse sample types. Large-scale reconstruction of viral genomes within specific taxonomic groups remains a lengthy, labor-intensive process constrained by fragmented assemblies, heterogeneous workflows, and the limitations of percent identity cut-offs for taxonomic placement. Here, we focused on Tobamovirus (family Virgaviridae), a genus that contains important emerging plant pathogens. Tobamoviruses are detectable in diverse environmental matrices and are thus expected to be present across a range of datasets. We mined global short-read datasets to uncover hidden tobamovirus diversity, combining expert curation with supervised machine learning to streamline the discovery of novel tobamoviruses. Using the Serratus PalmID tool, we first identified 253 candidate datasets that are most likely to contain novel tobamoviruses. We developed a reproducible Snakemake pipeline for quality control, de novo assembly, similarity searches, and preliminary taxonomic assignment, yielding 510 candidate tobamovirus contigs across 131 datasets. Following manual curation, we confirmed 228 tobamoviral contigs from 23 datasets based on BLAST similarity searches, coding sequence content, genome organization, and assessment of potential misassemblies. To expedite the curation process, we built a two-stage machine learning classifier of tobamoviral contigs. Based on alignment-derived features and sequence properties, each ORF is first scored to determine whether it is tobamoviral. ORF-level predictions are then merged into contig-level classification using stacked generalization. Through clustering and phylogenetic analyses, we identified at least 32 putative novel tobamoviruses in datasets derived from freshwater, wastewater, plants, animal gut, and soil. Most were placed within established Tobamovirus subclades, whereas a few highly divergent sequences formed distinct basal branches related to recently identified soil-associated sequences classified as Virgaviridae sp. These findings highlight the value of aquatic and wastewater systems for expanding our understanding of tobamoviral diversity and demonstrate how data mining and targeted curation can substantially expand recognized diversity within the genus. The workflow is readily adaptable to other viral taxa and supports continuous discovery as public datasets grow.

papers.title: RiboDFM: Robust RNA sequence design using backbone-conditioned discrete flow matching
papers.abstract: Designing RNA sequences that fold into predefined 3D structures is central to RNA engineering, yet it remains challenging due to the scarcity of experimentally determined structures and the complex sequence-structure relationships. Here, we present RiboDFM, a backbone-conditioned discrete flow-matching framework for RNA sequence design. RiboDFM progressively resolves fully masked sequences by integrating a geometric backbone encoder, an auxiliary base-pairing prediction head, and language model representations into a discrete flow sampler. To expand our training data, we supplemented experimental structures with a large-scale collection of trRosettaRNA2-predicted models. Across diverse benchmarks, RiboDFM achieves high sequence recovery and generates sequences with greater tertiary-structure self-consistency than existing methods. RiboDFM also performs strongly on aptamer-focused design tasks. Finally, beyond sequence generation, the nucleotide probabilities derived from RiboDFM' s flow trajectory serve as an intrinsic measure of sequence-structure compatibility. This enables reliable confidence estimation for designed sequences, as well as reference-free, zero-shot assessment of predicted structure models. Together, these results establish RiboDFM as an effective framework for structure-based RNA sequence design.

papers.title: Design of full-length agonist and antagonist antibodies for hard targets
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibodies have transformed modern medicine, yet conventional discovery relies on lengthy experimental workflows, offers limited control over how antibodies engage their targets, and struggles to deliver candidates across many important target classes. Despite recent advances in computational protein design, generating full-length antibodies with desired functional activity and favorable developability profiles remains challenging. Here we present an end-to-end computational design pipeline built around Pythia-1, an all-atom generative model that reasons jointly over amino acid sequence and three-dimensional atomic structure under explicit design constraints. We generated candidates in full-length human immunoglobulin G (IgG) format across 22 therapeutic targets spanning receptor ectodomains, cytokines, growth factors, and G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a particularly challenging target class for antibody discovery. Following a single computational design round, experimental screening of at most 48 candidates per target identified antibodies with single-digit nanomolar affinities for soluble proteins and single-digit nanomolar cell-binding EC50 values for GPCRs. The pipeline's ability to target specified epitopes and conformational states enabled the design of antibodies with agonist and antagonist activity. In vitro characterization demonstrated target-specific engagement and potent functional modulation, with single-digit nanomolar inhibitory potency in functional assays for a range of targets, including multiple GPCRs. To our knowledge, this study provides the first demonstration of both GPCR agonism and antagonism by de novo designed full-length IgG antibodies. We incorporated key developability and manufacturability requirements into the initial designs by conditioning generation on human germline frameworks and applying sequence constraints to limit known liabilities. The resulting antibody designs exhibited biophysical profiles comparable to or better than those of clinical-stage therapeutic controls. We provide the complete sequences of all lead candidates to support independent experimental validation and further development. Together, these findings demonstrate that our technology can deliver antibodies with programmable function and key properties expected of lead candidates, opening opportunities for first-in-class therapeutics against hard-to-drug targets.

papers.title: Cornealia: automated collective order analysis reveals density-dependent reorganization of donor corneal endothelium
papers.abstract: The corneal endothelium is a non-regenerative monolayer whose health determines transplant success, yet donor tissue is assessed only by single-cell metrics that ignore how the monolayer is organized collectively. A physics-based spring constant K, derived from the radial distribution function of cell positions, captures this collective order but has remained limited to semi-manual studies without physical interpretation. Here we present Cornealia, an automated pipeline for collective-order and intercellular-force analysis. In cultured endothelial cells, collective order declines with passaging and is higher under growth-factor conditions that preserve N-cadherin junctions, differences invisible to cell density and hexagonality. Across 2,177 donor cornea images from two cohorts, collective order, distinct from classical metrics, responds most to mechanical perturbation: corneas with endothelial cell density above 2,400 cells/mm^2 mostly gain order, whereas less dense ones lose it, on one curve shared by both cohorts. Reconstructed intercellular forces track these changes. This switch lies within the minimum donor densities used by eye banks, suggesting a mechanical basis for these clinical thresholds and establishing collective order as an automatable measure of endothelial quality.

papers.title: AntiOxiPred: Predicting Antioxidant Peptides using Machine Learning Techniques and BLAST
papers.abstract: Antioxidant peptides (AOPs) offer significant therapeutic potential in counteracting oxidative damage associated with chronic diseases. As AOPs gain market traction in cosmeceuticals, functional foods, and clinical trials for disease intervention, efficient computational methods are essential to accelerate their discovery. In this study, a systematic attempt has been made to develop a highly accurate and reliable method for predicting AOPs from their primary sequences. The dataset comprises 1,511 experimentally validated AOPs and 1,511 randomly generated non-AOPs, partitioned into 2,417 sequences for training and 606 for testing. First, we developed machine learning-based models using one-hot encoded (OHE) representations, sequence-derived compositional features, protein language model (PLM) embeddings, and feature fusion. Our CatBoost model, developed using selected fused features, achieved the best performance, with an AUC of 0.945 and an MCC of 0.788 on the independent testing dataset. An ensemble model combining CatBoost with BLAST achieved a peak AUC of 0.956 on the same testing dataset. Furthermore, our method outperformed existing state-of-the-art predictors when benchmarked on two external validation datasets comprising 150 peptides (75 AOPs and 75 non-AOPs) and 248 peptides (124 AOPs and 124 non-AOPs). AntiOxiPred (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/antioxipred/) is freely available as an interactive web server, a standalone package, and a pip-installable tool to support the scientific community.

papers.title: Characterization of heterogeneous bioinformatics training needs in the AI era
papers.abstract: Bioinformatics training providers serve heterogeneous audiences, a challenge sharpened by fast-evolving technologies such as generative artificial intelligence (AI). Analyzing training-needs surveys in aggregate can mask this heterogeneity. We present a network-based clustering protocol that groups respondents by the similarity of their Likert-type topic ratings: respondents form a Spearman correlation network, and community detection groups them into learner profiles with shared training needs, independent of demographics. We demonstrate the protocol on the 2026 SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) training needs survey (n=260), covering topics, barriers, and formats. We identified four interpretable learner profiles: AI and data, infectious disease genomics, functional genomics, and biochemistry, imaging & AI. Each had distinct topic priorities, barriers, and format preferences that an aggregate analysis hides. For example, LLM-based knowledge extraction ranked 2nd overall but only 16th in the infectious disease genomics profile, whereas phylogenetics ranked 17th overall but first there. Across profiles, AI/LLM skills and reproducible data practices were in high demand, whereas AI-assisted learning was, unexpectedly, the least preferred format. Because the protocol requires only a shared Likert scale, it is reusable for other training-needs assessments; the implementation is openly available. Profile-based curricula can target each group's topics, formats, and barriers.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.

papers.title: PHACTn enables training-free, context-independent inference of nucleotide variant tolerance across the genome
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of single-nucleotide variant (SNV) tolerability across the entire human genome remains a fundamental challenge in computational genomics, particularly for non-coding regions where the regulatory landscape is vast and poorly understood. Machine learning classifiers suffer from data circularity and demographic bias, while genomic language models demand massive computational resources and offer little biological interpretability. Here, we present PHACTn (Phylogeny-Aware Computing of Tolerance for nucleotide variants), a training-free, parameter-minimal method that infers nucleotide variant tolerability by traversing the mammalian phylogenetic tree and explicitly modeling the evolutionary independence of observed substitutions and their distance from the query species. With only 4 interpretable parameters, no training and no GPU requirement, PHACTn outperforms all evaluated tools on non-coding variants curated from both the ClinVar, and on non-coding variants potentially responsible for selected Mendelian diseases curated from OMIM. Additionally, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on variants within the informative range of alignment-based inference. These results establish that principled probabilistic phylogenetic modeling captures evolutionary constraint signals that large-scale sequence models fail to recover, offering a powerful, accessible, and mechanistically transparent alternative for genome-wide variant effect prediction.

papers.title: PI 3-kinase isoform p110α mediated FOXO1 inactivation protects against aortic aneurysm formation
papers.abstract: Aims: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are characterized by loss of contractile smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Regenerative approaches for AAAs should therefore aim at enriching aortic SMC content. We explored the role of PI 3-kinase isoform p110, a crucial regulator of cellular proliferation, survival and phenotype, for vascular integrity and AAA disease. Methods and results: Mice lacking p110 or FOXO1 in SMCs (sm-p110-/-, sm-FOXO1-/-) were exposed to the porcine pancreatic elastase (PPE) AAA model. Phenotypic alterations were examined by ultrasound, (immuno)histochemistry, transmission electron microscopy, functional and cellular assays, and single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) in tamoxifen-inducible ism-p110-/--eYFP lineage tracing mice. PPE treatment of sm-p110-/- mice yielded aggravated AAA formation compared to wild-type controls. AAA onset in sm-p110-/- aortae was facilitated by a subtle preexisting basal phenotype displaying smaller media area, impaired aortic wall structure, and diminished responsiveness to vasodilators. During AAA progression, PPE treated sm-p110-/- aortae were characterized by impaired vascular remodeling, reduced SMC content and medial cell proliferation, and increased elastic fiber breaks and ECM degradation. scRNA-seq revealed decreased content of proliferative and reparative SMC clusters and increased inflamed SMCs in ism-p110-/--eYFP mice. p110 deficient SMCs displayed impaired SMC proliferation, and production of elastin fibers. This phenotype was rescued by FOXO1 inactivation in p110-/- SMCs. FOXO1 deficiency in SMCs protected against AAA in PPE-treated sm-FOXO1-/- mice. Pharmacological activation of p110 ameliorated AAA in wild type mice but not in sm-FOXO1-/- mice. Relevance of p110/FOXO1 signaling in human AAA disease was indicated in patient samples. Conclusions: p110-mediated inactivation of FOXO1 in SMCs protects against AAA disease and contributes to maintaining aortic wall homoeostasis. p110 signaling promotes transition into proliferating and reparative SMC phenotypes while attenuating de-differentiation into inflammatory SMC subtypes. Our findings identify (pharmacological) activation of p110 signaling in SMCs as a new therapeutic strategy to promote prevention and regeneration of AAA disease.

papers.title: Iterative Refinement for Structural Optimization of De Novo Protein Sequences
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce an iterative refinement procedure that substitutes individual amino acid residues in a predicted protein sequence to minimize structural error; substitutions are guided by a weighted composite score of global evaluation metrics including the TM-score, GDT-TS, and RMSD. Starting from an initial sequence prediction produced by a structure-aware graph neural network (GNN) [5], the refinement procedure evaluates candidate amino acid substitutions at each position by folding the modified sequence with ESMFold [9] and accepting substitutions that satisfy both a global structural improvement criterion and a local displacement threshold. Evaluated on a matched sample of 224 proteins, this set of methods reduced mean RMSD from 8.097 [A] to 4.570 [A] relative to the model's initial prediction, a 43.6% reduction, with corresponding reductions of 46.2% relative to ProteinMPNN and 27.2% relative to native ESMFolded sequences; these differences were statistically significant by paired t-test (p < 0.001). Our results show that post-prediction iterative refinement can significantly improve the structural accuracy of de novo protein sequences.

papers.title: Optimized dosing of spatially heterogeneous radiopharmaceutical therapy reprograms poorly immunogenic tumors to enhance response to immune checkpoint blockade
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are ineffective in patients with poorly immunogenic tumors due to exclusion or exhaustion of effector T cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and/or inadequate priming of tumor-specific T cells. Preclinical and clinical studies suggest that radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) may overcome such challenges, but an optimal approach to RPT dosing has not been clarified in combination with ICIs. Conventional RPT dosimetry emphasizes mean absorbed radiation doses in tumors and normal tissues, neglecting the spatial distribution of this dose in the TME. We hypothesize that RPT dose heterogeneity in tumors may be leveraged to initiate spatially restricted immuno-radiobiological effects in TME that potentiate antitumor immunity when injecting an activity that delivers high dose (V10%>20 Gy) while also preserving low dose regions (V90%<2.5 Gy) in the TME and not inducing systemic lymphopenia. In studies using lutetium-177 RPT in combination with ICIs, administered activities that met these dosimetric optimization metrics occurred at different mean tumor doses for different RPT agents and different models, yet each achieved therapeutic efficacy in poorly immunogenic murine tumors. Spatial transcriptomics at day 7 after RPT revealed heterogeneous distribution of tumor cell markers with distinct dose-response profiles and localization of dendritic cell (DC) migratory markers in regions of moderate/high dose response marker expression. Combination therapy sustained conventional type 1 DC (cDC1) activation in tumor draining lymph nodes and promoted systemic expansion of antigen-specific CD8 T cells, while serial biopsies revealed effector T cell recruitment and inflammatory cytokine expression in the TME. Optimized intratumoral dose heterogeneity may enable and predict response to ICIs when combined with RPT in tumors not responding adequately to ICIs alone.

papers.title: Beyond profiles: supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings
papers.abstract: Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey {beta}-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.

papers.title: De novo Protein Generating Model via Structure-Aware Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The focus of this paper is to create a protein conformation prediction model that is optimized for structural accuracy rather than sequence recovery. To achieve this goal, we created a graph neural network (GNN) [19] for the design of computational proteins that integrates differentiable structure prediction through ESMFold [13] via a structural loss function, allowing direct optimization of the 3D conformational accuracy. Our model takes protein backbone coordinates as input and predicts an amino acid sequence using a composite loss that heavily weights structural similarity. On a matched evaluation sample, our model achieves structural precision (RMSD, TM-score, and GDT-TS) that is statistically indistinguishable from ProteinMPNN, a leading sequence recovery-focused method, despite training with no direct sequence recovery supervision and substantially lower native sequence recovery. Our results demonstrate that sequence recovery is not necessary to achieve competitive structural accuracy and that proteins can possess multiple non-unique solutions, suggesting that protein sequence prediction models may perform comparably well under purely structural conformation training. This distinction in training data and model structure allows for the training of a protein-generating model on non-natural proteins. Creating a model designed for de novo protein generation.

papers.title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling
papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3' UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.

papers.title: AI-based prognosis and chemotherapy benefit in node-positive, HR+ breast cancer: a blinded external validation on SWOG-8814 trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy varies among patients with postmenopausal, node-positive, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Genomic assays identify patients likely to benefit from chemotherapy but are expensive and tissue consuming. AI-enabled biomarkers may provide scalable alternatives. We performed a blinded external evaluation of Ataraxis Breast CTX, a causal multi-modal AI model that integrates H&E images with clinical variables, in the phase III SWOG-8814 trial. MethodsThe analytic cohort comprised 677 patients (46% of the 1477 enrolled) with digitized H&E slides. Two CTX scores were evaluated: a histology-only score and a multi-modal score integrating pathology features with clinical variables. CTX weights and thresholds were locked before evaluation and SWOG-8814 data were not used for retraining. Predictions were generated blinded to outcomes and provided to SWOG for validation. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival (DFS), matching the primary endpoint of the trial. FindingsThe histology-only score was prognostic for DFS (HR = 1.36, 95% CI = 1.22-1.51) and added prognostic information beyond clinical variables alone (p < 0.001). The multi-modal score showed a stronger association with DFS (HR = 1.60, 95% CI = 1.44-1.78, p < 0.001) and greater discrimination than the histology-only score (C-index 0.66 vs 0.59). In exploratory analyses, modeled as a continuous score, CTX-benefit showed a treatment-by-biomarker interaction of HR of 0.82 (0.64-1.04, p = 0.053) for CET versus ET. The chemotherapy effect on DFS was numerically larger in the high-benefit subgroup (n = 480, HR = 0.79, 95% CI = 0.59-1.05) compared to the low-benefit subgroup (n = 197, HR = 0.91, 95% CI = 0.49-1.68). InterpretationIn this blinded validation, CTX was significantly associated with DFS, supporting its prognostic value. In exploratory analyses, CTX demonstrated suggestive evidence of a treatment-by-biomarker interaction for chemotherapy benefit. These findings support further prospective validation of CTX as a tissue-sparing tool for recurrence-risk assessment and treatment selection. FundingNational Cancer Institute, The Hope Foundation for Cancer Research, and Ataraxis AI. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for studies published between Jan 1, 2016, and Sept 1, 2026, using the terms ("digital pathology" OR "deep learning" OR "artificial intelligence") AND ("hematoxylin" OR "haematoxylin" OR "H&E") AND "breast cancer" AND ("chemotherapy benefit" OR "predictive biomarker"), without language restrictions. Multiple AI models based on H&E-stained whole-slide images, with or without clinical variables, have been developed to estimate recurrence risk in early hormone receptor-positive (HR+) breast cancer. However, robust evidence for AI-based prediction of chemotherapy benefit remains limited as most models either infer the 21-gene Recurrence Score or estimate baseline recurrence risk. To date, n

papers.title: SC-MAPS: Image-based deep learning for bacterial identification and antibiotic-susceptibility testing
papers.abstract: Rapid bacterial identification could help guide antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), but image-based classification must generalise across bacterial strains. We developed SC-MAPS, a multichannel microscopy dataset comprising 916,435 single cells from 13 bacterial species, with independent strains reserved for evaluation. Combining phase-contrast and fluorescence information using deep learning achieved 65.4% single-cell species-classification accuracy on held-out strains. To assess whether imperfect species predictions retained useful information for downstream testing, we defined eight antimicrobial-resistance-informed AST-routing groups. Pooling species probabilities increased routing accuracy to 77.1%, rising to 91.1% when predictions from five cells were combined and 96.2% with 20 cells. Synthetic mixtures revealed limitations in minority-species recovery, while exploratory analysis of unseen organisms demonstrated the potential for out-of-distribution detection. SC-MAPS provides a framework for investigating transferable bacterial phenotypes and developing image-based identification and AST-routing strategies.

papers.title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS: High-fidelity gEneration via Latent Interpolant Conditional Synthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing >600K SNPs to 4,096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to real genotypes than existing haplotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.

papers.title: Active Learning of Conditional Generative Models via the Transport Neural Tangent Kernel
papers.abstract: Many high-throughput scientific experiments produce distributional outputs, requiring conditional generative models to interpret the data, and to predict outcomes at new inputs. Acquiring experimental data at new conditions (e.g., for a new antigen or a new cell type) is often expensive, motivating the need for automated experimental design methods. However, existing active learning frameworks are limited as they assume scalar or vector-valued outputs. We first show that the Wasserstein test risk of a conditional generative task decomposes into a mean term and a shape term, demonstrating why mean-based active learning is blind to distributional shape. To capture both, we propose the transport Neural Tangent Kernel (tNTK), a tractable kernel that measures how sensitive a generative model's predicted distribution is with respect to its parameters. The tNTK recovers the standard NTK in the deterministic limit and upper-bounds the posterior Fréchet variance of the prediction under small parameter perturbations. It admits a closed-form expression for affine Gaussian transport and tractable Monte Carlo estimators otherwise. Treating the tNTK as the covariance function of a Gaussian process, we greedily select inputs that minimize the total GP posterior variance across the pool, yielding a distribution-aware active learning strategy. We evaluate this strategy across four classes of conditional generative models, including conditional flow matching and conditional Monge gap, on synthetic distributions, intent-labeled sentences, and single-cell perturbation responses. In these experiments, the tNTK outperforms the baseline NTK computed from the conditional mean, demonstrating the value of distribution-aware active learning for generative-modeling tasks.

papers.title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning for Generative Flexible Docking
papers.abstract: Flexible docking is a highly practical task, aiming to predict the joint configuration of a protein-ligand complex from a protein apo structure and a ligand SMILES string. Diffusion and flow-based generative models have made this task tractable by modeling the posterior distribution over the ligand pose and the protein conformation conditioned on the apo input. The central challenge, however, remains the long-tailed apo-to-holo structure shift, where a small fraction of protein undergo large conformational changes. In this work, motivated by the practical observation that downweighting large shift examples improves generalization, and by the mixed nature of the long tail consisting of genuinely difficult examples and noisy ones, we propose to use curriculum learning for this task, gradually incorporating large conformational change examples during training. With a linear pacing function, we show that an existing method can be strongly enhanced. On the PDBBind ESMFold apo benchmark, with relaxation and confidence-based pose selection, the resulting model GCLDock achieves a 46.52% top-1 success rate (ligand RMSD less than 2A) and 40.26% when additionally requiring PoseBusters validity, outperforming existing baselines.

papers.title: The promising role of new molecular biomarkers in prostate cancer: from coding and non-coding genes to artificial intelligence approaches
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Risk stratification or progression in prostate cancer is performed with the support of clinical-pathological data such as the sum of the Gleason score and serum levels PSA. For several decades, methods aimed at the early detection of prostate cancer have included the determination of PSA serum levels. The aim of this systematic review is to provide an overview about recent advances in the discovery of new molecular biomarkers through transcriptomics, genomics and artificial intelligence that are expected to improve clinical management of the prostate cancer patient. METHODS: An exhaustive search was conducted by Pubmed, Google Scholar and Connected Papers using keywords relating to the genetics, genomics and artificial intelligence in prostate cancer, it includes "biomarkers", "non-coding RNAs", "lncRNAs", "microRNAs", "repetitive sequence", "prognosis", "prediction", "whole-genome sequencing", "RNA-Seq", "transcriptome", "machine learning", and "deep learning". RESULTS: New advances, including the search for changes in novel biomarkers such as mRNAs, microRNAs, lncRNAs, and repetitive sequences, are expected to contribute to an earlier and accurate diagnosis for each patient in the context of precision medicine, thus improving the prognosis and quality of life of patients. We analyze several aspects that are relevant for prostate cancer including its new molecular markers associated with diagnosis, prognosis, and prediction to therapy and how bioinformatic approaches such as machine learning and deep learning can contribute to clinic. Furthermore, we also include current techniques that will allow an earlier diagnosis, such as Spatial Transcriptomics, Exome Sequencing, and Whole-Genome Sequencing. CONCLUSION: Transcriptomic and genomic analysis have contributed to generate knowledge in the field of prostate carcinogenesis, new information about coding and non-coding genes as biomarkers has emerged. Synergies created by the implementation of artificial intelligence to analyze and understand sequencing data have allowed the development of clinical strategies that facilitate decision-making and improve personalized management in prostate cancer.

papers.title: Predicting transcriptional responses to novel chemical perturbations using deep generative model for drug discovery
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding transcriptional responses to chemical perturbations is central for drug discovery, but exhaustive experimental high-throughput screening of disease and compound combinations is unfeasible. To overcome this limitation, here we present a perturbation-conditioned deep generative model named PRnet for predicting transcriptional responses to novel chemical perturbations that were never experimentally perturbed at bulk and single-cell levels. Evaluation indicated that PRnet outperformed alternative methods in predicting responses across novel compounds, pathways, and cell lines. PRnet enables gene-level response interpretation and novel compounds screening for diseases based on gene signatures. PRnet further identified and experimentally tested novel compounds candidates against small cell lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Lastly, PRnet generated a large-scale integration atlas of perturbation profiles, covering 88 cell lines and 52 tissues perturbed by various screening compound libraries. PRnet provided a robust and scalable candidate recommendation workflow and has successfully recommended drug candidates for 233 different diseases based on the atlas. Overall, PRnet is an effective and valuable tool for cell- and gene-based therapeutics screening.

papers.title: Image-based consensus molecular subtype (imCMS) classification of colorectal cancer using deep learning
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Complex phenotypes captured on histological slides represent the biological processes at play in individual cancers, but the link to underlying molecular classification has not been clarified or systematised. In colorectal cancer (CRC), histological grading is a poor predictor of disease progression, and consensus molecular subtypes (CMSs) cannot be distinguished without gene expression profiling. We hypothesise that image analysis is a cost-effective tool to associate complex features of tissue organisation with molecular and outcome data and to resolve unclassifiable or heterogeneous cases. In this study, we present an image-based approach to predict CRC CMS from standard H&E sections using deep learning. DESIGN: Training and evaluation of a neural network were performed using a total of n=1206 tissue sections with comprehensive multi-omic data from three independent datasets (training on FOCUS trial, n=278 patients; test on rectal cancer biopsies, GRAMPIAN cohort, n=144 patients; and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), n=430 patients). Ground truth CMS calls were ascertained by matching random forest and single sample predictions from CMS classifier. RESULTS: Image-based CMS (imCMS) accurately classified slides in unseen datasets from TCGA (n=431 slides, AUC)=0.84) and rectal cancer biopsies (n=265 slides, AUC=0.85). imCMS spatially resolved intratumoural heterogeneity and provided secondary calls correlating with bioinformatic prediction from molecular data. imCMS classified samples previously unclassifiable by RNA expression profiling, reproduced the expected correlations with genomic and epigenetic alterations and showed similar prognostic associations as transcriptomic CMS. CONCLUSION: This study shows that a prediction of RNA expression classifiers can be made from H&E images, opening the door to simple, cheap and reliable biological stratification within routine workflows.

papers.title: ACTINN: automated identification of cell types in single cell RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Abstract Cell type identification is one of the major goals in single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Current methods for assigning cell types typically involve the use of unsupervised clustering, the identification of signature genes in each cluster, followed by a manual lookup of these genes in the literature and databases to assign cell types. However, there are several limitations associated with these approaches, such as unwanted sources of variation that influence clustering and a lack of canonical markers for certain cell types. Here, we present ACTINN (Automated Cell Type Identification using Neural Networks), which employs a neural network with 3 hidden layers, trains on datasets with predefined cell types, and predicts cell types for other datasets based on the trained parameters. We trained the neural network on a mouse cell type atlas (Tabula Muris Atlas) and a human immune cell dataset, and used it to predict cell types for mouse leukocytes, human PBMCs and human T cell sub types. The results showed that our neural network is fast and accurate, and should therefore be a useful tool to complement existing scRNA-seq pipelines. Author Summary Single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides high resolution profiling of the transcriptomes of individual cells, which inevitably results in high volumes of data that require complex data processing pipelines. Usually, one of the first steps in the analysis of scRNA-seq is to assign individual cells to known cell types. To accomplish this, traditional methods first group the cells into different clusters, then find marker genes, and finally use these to manually assign cell types for each cluster. Thus these methods require prior knowledge of cell type canonical markers, and some level of subjectivity to make the cell type assignments. As a result, the process is often laborious and requires domain specific expertise, which is a barrier for inexperienced users. By contrast, our neural network ACTINN automatically learns the features for each predefined cell type and uses these features to predict cell types for individual cells. This approach is computationally efficient and requires no domain expertise of the tissues being studied. We believe ACTINN allows users to rapidly identify cell types in their datasets, thus rendering the analysis of their scRNA-seq datasets more efficient.

papers.title: DeLTA: Automated cell segmentation, tracking, and lineage reconstruction using deep learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Microscopy image analysis is a major bottleneck in quantification of single-cell microscopy data, typically requiring human supervision and curation, which limit both accuracy and throughput. To address this, we developed a deep learning-based image analysis pipeline that performs segmentation, tracking, and lineage reconstruction. Our analysis focuses on time-lapse movies of Escherichia coli cells trapped in a “mother machine” microfluidic device, a scalable platform for long-term single-cell analysis that is widely used in the field. While deep learning has been applied to cell segmentation problems before, our approach is fundamentally innovative in that it also uses machine learning to perform cell tracking and lineage reconstruction. With this framework we are able to get high fidelity results (1% error rate), without human supervision. Further, the algorithm is fast, with complete analysis of a typical frame containing ∼150 cells taking <700msec. The framework is not constrained to a particular experimental set up and has the potential to generalize to time-lapse images of other organisms or different experimental configurations. These advances open the door to a myriad of applications including real-time tracking of gene expression and high throughput analysis of strain libraries at single-cell resolution. Author Summary Automated microscopy experiments can generate massive data sets, allowing for detailed analysis of cell physiology and properties such as gene expression. In particular, dynamic measurements of gene expression with time-lapse microscopy have proved invaluable for understanding how gene regulatory networks operate. However, image analysis remains a key bottleneck in the analysis pipeline, typically requiring human supervision and a posteriori processing. Recently, machine learning-based approaches have ushered in a new era of rapid, unsupervised image analysis. In this work, we use and repurpose the U-Net deep learning algorithm to develop an image processing pipeline that can not only accurately identify the location of cells in an image, but also track them over time as they grow and divide. As an application, we focus on multi-hour time-lapse movies of bacteria growing in a microfluidic device. Our algorithm is accurate and fast, with error rates near 1% and requiring less than a second to analyze a typical movie frame. This increase in speed and fidelity has the potential to open new experimental avenues, e.g. where images are analyzed on-the-fly so that experimental conditions can be updated in real time.

papers.title: Identifying multicellular spatiotemporal organization of cells with SpaceFlow
papers.abstract: One major challenge in analyzing spatial transcriptomic datasets is to simultaneously incorporate the cell transcriptome similarity and their spatial locations. Here, we introduce SpaceFlow, which generates spatially-consistent low-dimensional embeddings by incorporating both expression similarity and spatial information using spatially regularized deep graph networks. Based on the embedding, we introduce a pseudo-Spatiotemporal Map that integrates the pseudotime concept with spatial locations of the cells to unravel spatiotemporal patterns of cells. By comparing with multiple existing methods on several spatial transcriptomic datasets at both spot and single-cell resolutions, SpaceFlow is shown to produce a robust domain segmentation and identify biologically meaningful spatiotemporal patterns. Applications of SpaceFlow reveal evolving lineage in heart developmental data and tumor-immune interactions in human breast cancer data. Our study provides a flexible deep learning framework to incorporate spatiotemporal information in analyzing spatial transcriptomic data.

papers.title: Pan-cancer proteomic map of 949 human cell lines
papers.abstract: The proteome provides unique insights into disease biology beyond the genome and transcriptome. A lack of large proteomic datasets has restricted the identification of new cancer biomarkers. Here, proteomes of 949 cancer cell lines across 28 tissue types are analyzed by mass spectrometry. Deploying a workflow to quantify 8,498 proteins, these data capture evidence of cell-type and post-transcriptional modifications. Integrating multi-omics, drug response, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene essentiality screens with a deep learning-based pipeline reveals thousands of protein biomarkers of cancer vulnerabilities that are not significant at the transcript level. The power of the proteome to predict drug response is very similar to that of the transcriptome. Further, random downsampling to only 1,500 proteins has limited impact on predictive power, consistent with protein networks being highly connected and co-regulated. This pan-cancer proteomic map (ProCan-DepMapSanger) is a comprehensive resource available at https://cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk.

papers.title: Modeling Sporadic Alzheimer's Disease in Human Brain Organoids under Serum Exposure
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with no cure. Huge efforts have been made to develop anti-AD drugs in the past decades. However, all drug development programs for disease-modifying therapies have failed. Possible reasons for the high failure rate include incomplete understanding of complex pathophysiology of AD, especially sporadic AD (sAD), and species difference between humans and animal models used in preclinical studies. In this study, sAD is modeled using human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived 3D brain organoids. Because the blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage is a well-known risk factor for AD, brain organoids are exposed to human serum to mimic the serum exposure consequence of BBB breakdown in AD patient brains. The serum-exposed brain organoids are able to recapitulate AD-like pathologies, including increased amyloid beta (Aβ) aggregates and phosphorylated microtubule-associated tau protein (p-Tau) level, synaptic loss, and impaired neural network. Serum exposure increases Aβ and p-Tau levels through inducing beta-secretase 1 (BACE) and glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha / beta (GSK3α/β) levels, respectively.
